items.prompt: Which signal would tell you exactly what happened for one specific failing checkout request?
choices: A metric
A log
A dashboard alert threshold
A load balancer health check
items.explanation: Logs are discrete, per-event records — they're the signal built to answer 'what exactly happened for this one thing,' not metrics (aggregate numbers) or health checks (up/down only).

items.prompt: Which signal would tell you whether checkout error rate spiked in the last five minutes, across all requests?
choices: A single log line
A metric
A trace for one request
A stack trace
items.explanation: Metrics are aggregated numbers over time (counters, gauges, histograms) — exactly what's needed to answer 'how much / how often across everything,' not a single request's detail.

items.prompt: Which signal would tell you which of four services a slow checkout request spent the most time in?
choices: A trace
A log level
A counter metric
An error message string
items.explanation: A trace follows one request across service boundaries and shows where time was spent in each — that's specifically what tracing answers, distinct from a log (one event) or a counter (a running total).

items.prompt: What is the main practical advantage of a structured (JSON) log line over a free-text string like console.log("here")?
choices: It takes less disk space than plain text
It can be filtered and queried by field, not just searched as text
It runs faster at write time than string concatenation
It doesn't need a timestamp
items.explanation: The value of structure is queryability — 'show me every error where attempt >= 3' is a field filter against structured logs, and effectively impossible against a pile of free-text sentences.

items.prompt: A team has thousands of production log lines like "user checkout failed, retrying". Why is this hard to use during an incident even though it's readable?
choices: It has no consistent fields to filter or aggregate on across lines
It's written in the wrong programming language
console.log is deprecated in modern browsers
It doesn't use enough exclamation marks to signal severity
items.explanation: A free-text sentence is fine to read once, live — the problem is scale: with no consistent fields, there's nothing to filter, group, or count on later, which is exactly what's needed during an incident.

items.prompt: A retry attempt fails once but then succeeds on the second try, with no user-visible impact. What log level fits best?
choices: debug
warn
fatal
info only, never log a failed retry
items.explanation: warn fits 'something unexpected happened but the system recovered on its own' — a retry that failed once and then succeeded is exactly that case, not routine (info) and not user-impacting (error).

items.prompt: A process hits an unrecoverable error and is about to crash. What log level fits best?
choices: debug
info
fatal
warn
items.explanation: fatal is specifically for the process itself being unable to continue — a crash or forced exit — which is more severe than error (an operation failed but the process keeps running).

items.prompt: A request completes normally and nothing unusual happened. What log level fits a routine record of this event?
choices: error
fatal
info
warn
items.explanation: info is for routine events worth a permanent record — a request completing normally is the textbook case; error/warn/fatal are reserved for something going wrong to varying degrees.

items.prompt: What does it mean for a system to have good observability?
choices: It never has bugs in production
You can answer new questions about its behavior using only data it already produces, without shipping new code
It logs every function call at debug level in production
It has a status page customers can check
items.explanation: Observability is specifically about answering questions you didn't anticipate, using data already being recorded — the opposite of the Scenario's loop of guessing, adding a print statement, and redeploying.

items.prompt: An engineer needs to add a new console.log line and redeploy just to answer 'which service did this request fail in?' What does this indicate about the system?
choices: The system has excellent observability
The system's observability is insufficient — that question should be answerable from existing data
The bug is unfixable without a rewrite
The team should switch programming languages
items.explanation: Needing to instrument-and-redeploy just to answer a basic question about a request's path is the exact symptom of missing observability — the data to answer it should already exist.

items.prompt: Why is it usually a bad idea to leave debug-level logging enabled everywhere in production, all the time?
choices: debug logs are illegal to store under most data-protection laws
The volume buries the important lines and adds real storage/processing cost
debug logs can only be written to a terminal, never to a file
It causes the application to run in a slower, unoptimized build mode
items.explanation: The problem is volume and cost, not legality or performance mode — an always-on debug firehose makes the genuinely important error/warn lines harder to find and costs real storage and processing.

items.prompt: What's a reasonable way to use debug-level logging in production when investigating a specific issue?
choices: Enable it everywhere, permanently, just in case
Enable it narrowly — one service, ideally one request or a short time window — then turn it back off
Never enable it in production under any circumstances
Replace all info-level logs with debug-level logs
items.explanation: Debug logging is most useful scoped tightly — one service, one request, a short window — rather than left on everywhere permanently, which just recreates the haystack problem it's meant to help solve.

items.prompt: A team logs every function entry and exit at debug level, always on, in a high-traffic service. What is the most likely consequence?
choices: Faster incident response, since every detail is captured
High storage/processing cost and error-level lines becoming harder to find among the noise
No consequence — logging has no measurable cost
The service automatically becomes more secure
items.explanation: Always-on debug logging at high traffic is expensive and counterproductive — it drowns the signal (errors, warnings) in noise instead of making incidents easier to resolve.

items.prompt: What problem does attaching the same correlation/request ID to every service's log lines for one request solve?
choices: It makes the request run faster
It lets you reconstruct one request's full story across independently-logging services
It encrypts the log lines for that request
It removes the need for log levels
items.explanation: A shared ID is what turns several services' independent log streams into one queryable, ordered story for a single request — it doesn't affect speed, encryption, or levels.

items.prompt: A request passes through service A, then B, then C. Service B forgets to forward the correlation ID to C. What happens to C's logs for that request?
choices: C's logs are automatically tagged anyway, since the ID is global
C's logs become orphaned — readable, but not linkable back to the same request as A and B
C refuses to process the request
A and B's logs get deleted
items.explanation: The ID only connects services that actually forward it — a dropped ID at any hop breaks the chain from that point on, leaving the downstream service's logs disconnected from the rest of the story.

items.prompt: Where should a correlation/trace ID for a request typically be generated?
choices: At the very first point the request enters the system
Independently by every service, each generating its own
Only by the database layer
Only when an error actually occurs
items.explanation: Generating it once at entry (e.g. the API gateway) and forwarding it downstream is what makes it a single shared thread through the whole request — independent per-service IDs wouldn't connect anything.

items.prompt: In a trace, what does a span's parentSpanId represent?
choices: The service that will handle the next request
The span that caused this span to start — the unit of work that called it
The user who initiated the original request
The log level of the span
items.explanation: parentSpanId links a span back to whichever span called it, the same way a call stack tracks who called whom — this is what lets a trace viewer reconstruct a nested timeline.

items.prompt: Two unrelated spans from different services are accidentally given the same parentSpanId. What's the practical consequence?
choices: The trace viewer crashes and shows nothing
The trace renders, but misrepresents which service actually made which call — a subtly wrong story, not a broken one
Nothing — parentSpanId is purely cosmetic and ignored by trace viewers
Both spans get merged into a single span automatically
items.explanation: A trace tree is only as trustworthy as its parent references — a wrong parent doesn't crash anything, it just draws the timeline as if the wrong service made the call, misleading anyone trying to attribute latency or duplicate calls correctly.

items.prompt: Which metric type would you use to track the current number of active database connections, which can go up or down?
choices: Counter
Gauge
Histogram
Log
items.explanation: A gauge is a value that can move in either direction — exactly right for 'currently active connections,' unlike a counter (only increases) or a histogram (a distribution of many values).

items.prompt: Which metric type would you use to compute p99 request latency?
choices: Counter
Gauge
Histogram
A single log line
items.explanation: A percentile requires a distribution of values over time, which is what a histogram tracks — a counter only sums, and a gauge only reports a single current value.

items.prompt: Which metric type would you use to track the total number of requests served since the process started?
choices: Gauge
Histogram
Counter
Trace
items.explanation: A counter only ever increases and is exactly right for a running total like 'requests served since start' — a gauge would be wrong since the value never legitimately decreases here.

items.prompt: Why is adding a userId label to a request-count metric risky, when adding a statusCode label to the same metric usually isn't?
choices: userId values are longer strings, which is a formatting problem
statusCode has a small, bounded set of values; userId is effectively unbounded, creating a new time series per user
userId is a security risk to log at all, while statusCode never is
Metrics don't support string labels, only numeric ones
items.explanation: Cardinality is about the number of distinct label-value combinations — statusCode has roughly a dozen values, while userId can have millions, each becoming its own stored time series.

items.prompt: A metric is labeled by both route (~40 values) and statusCode (~10 values). Roughly how many distinct time series does this create?
choices: About 50
About 400
About 4
Exactly 1, since it's still one metric name
items.explanation: Cardinality multiplies across labels — roughly 40 routes times 10 status codes is about 400 distinct combinations, each stored as its own time series, even though it's conceptually 'one metric.'

items.prompt: Per-request detail like a specific requestId is needed for debugging. Where does it belong instead of as a metric label?
choices: Nowhere — it should never be recorded at all
On logs and traces, which are built to hold per-event detail cheaply
As a metric label, since more detail is always better
Only in the database, never in observability data
items.explanation: Logs and traces are designed to carry high-cardinality, per-event detail; metrics are designed to stay cheap by staying low-cardinality — using each signal for what it's built for avoids the cardinality blow-up.

items.prompt: A metric counter is cheap to store partly because of what trade-off?
choices: It discards per-request detail and only keeps an aggregate number
It only runs once per day
It is stored on a different, cheaper kind of hard drive automatically
It compresses log lines using a special algorithm
items.explanation: A counter's cheapness comes directly from throwing away per-request identity — it doesn't remember which requests it counted, only the total, which is exactly what makes it fast and cheap.

items.prompt: If a metric already shows checkout error rate spiked at 14:02, why might you still need a trace or logs afterward?
choices: You wouldn't — the metric already tells you everything necessary
The metric shows *that* something spiked, but not *which* requests or *why* — that detail lives in logs and traces
Metrics and traces show exactly the same information, just in different formats
Traces are only used before an incident, never after
items.explanation: Metrics summarize 'how much/how often'; they don't carry per-request causal detail. Confirming *which* requests failed and *why* still requires dropping down to logs or a trace for a specific request.

items.prompt: Implement shouldLog(level, minLevel) so it returns true only when level's rank is greater than or equal to minLevel's rank, using the given LEVELS ranking.

tests.description: info passes when minLevel is info
debug is dropped when minLevel is info
error always passes a lower minLevel
warn is dropped when minLevel is error

items.explanation: Comparing numeric ranks is what makes level filtering a single comparison instead of a chain of special cases — any level at or above the configured threshold passes, anything below is dropped.
items.reference:
🔢 Ranks — debug:10, info:20, warn:30, error:40, fatal:50
✅ Rule — only log when the level's rank is ≥ the configured minimum

Why: filtering before formatting avoids paying to serialize lines that get thrown away anyway.

items.prompt: Implement countLoggable(levels, minLevel) that returns how many entries in the levels array would actually be logged at the given minLevel, using the given LEVELS ranking.

tests.description: counts only warn and error at minLevel warn
counts everything at minLevel debug
counts nothing when minLevel exceeds all entries

items.explanation: The same rank comparison used to filter a single line generalizes directly to filtering a whole array — computing the threshold once and reusing it avoids redundant lookups.
items.reference:
🔢 Ranks — debug:10, info:20, warn:30, error:40, fatal:50
✅ Rule — only log when the level's rank is ≥ the configured minimum

Why: filtering before formatting avoids paying to serialize lines that get thrown away anyway.

items.prompt: Implement createLogger({ minLevel }).log(level, msg) so it returns null for anything below minLevel, and otherwise returns an object with { level, msg }.

tests.description: drops debug when minLevel is info
keeps info when minLevel is info
keeps fatal regardless of minLevel

items.explanation: Returning null for a dropped line — instead of building and then discarding a record — is what avoids paying formatting cost for lines nobody will ever read, which matters once volume is real.
items.reference:
🔢 Ranks — debug:10, info:20, warn:30, error:40, fatal:50
✅ Rule — only log when the level's rank is ≥ the configured minimum

Why: filtering before formatting avoids paying to serialize lines that get thrown away anyway.

items.prompt: Implement forwardRequest(requestId, fromService, toService) so it returns a plain object representing the outbound call, tagging it with the same requestId it received.

tests.description: carries the same requestId forward
records the correct hop

items.explanation: Nothing forwards a correlation ID automatically — some explicit mechanism (a function argument here, an HTTP header in real systems) has to carry it across every call boundary, or the chain breaks at that hop.
items.reference:
🆔 Generated once — at the first entry point into the system
➡️ Forwarded explicitly — on every downstream call, by every hop

Why: a correlation ID only connects the services that actually pass it along — one dropped hop breaks the chain from that point on.

items.prompt: Implement buildRequestChain(requestId, hops) where hops is an array of service names in order (e.g. ['gateway','auth','payment']). Return an array of { requestId, fromService, toService } objects for each consecutive pair.

tests.description: builds one hop for two services
builds two hops for three services
every hop shares the same requestId

items.explanation: Every hop in the chain gets tagged with the exact same requestId — this is the mechanism that lets a later query filter every service's logs down to one request's full story, in order.
items.reference:
🆔 Generated once — at the first entry point into the system
➡️ Forwarded explicitly — on every downstream call, by every hop

Why: a correlation ID only connects the services that actually pass it along — one dropped hop breaks the chain from that point on.

items.prompt: Implement spanDuration(span) that returns endedAt - startedAt, or null if the span hasn't ended yet (endedAt is null).

tests.description: returns null for an unfinished span
computes duration for a finished span

items.explanation: A span's duration is only meaningful once it has actually ended — returning null for an in-flight span avoids reporting a fake, misleading duration for work that isn't finished yet.
items.reference:
🌳 parentSpanId — links a span back to whichever span called it
⏱️ duration — endedAt minus startedAt, once the span ends

Why: a trace viewer reconstructs the nested timeline purely from these parent references — a wrong one draws the wrong story without crashing anything.

items.prompt: Implement isChildOf(span, potentialParent) that returns true if span.parentSpanId matches potentialParent.spanId.

tests.description: true for a real parent/child pair
false for an unrelated span
false for a root span with no parent

items.explanation: This is exactly the relationship a trace viewer uses to reconstruct the nested timeline — a span is a child of whichever span's spanId matches its own parentSpanId, nothing more elaborate than that.
items.reference:
🌳 parentSpanId — links a span back to whichever span called it
⏱️ duration — endedAt minus startedAt, once the span ends

Why: a trace viewer reconstructs the nested timeline purely from these parent references — a wrong one draws the wrong story without crashing anything.

items.prompt: Implement findChildren(spans, parentSpanId) that returns every span in the array whose parentSpanId matches the given parentSpanId.

tests.description: finds direct children of a span
tests.expr: expect(findChildren([{ spanId: 'a', parentSpanId: 'root' }, { spanId: 'b', parentSpanId: 'other' }], 'root').map(s => s.spanId)).toEqual(['a'])

tests.description: returns empty array when there are no children
finds multiple children

items.explanation: Filtering by parentSpanId is the building block a trace viewer uses repeatedly, top-down, to walk the whole span tree one level of nesting at a time.
items.reference:
🌳 parentSpanId — links a span back to whichever span called it
⏱️ duration — endedAt minus startedAt, once the span ends

Why: a trace viewer reconstructs the nested timeline purely from these parent references — a wrong one draws the wrong story without crashing anything.

items.prompt: Implement shouldSample({ isError, sampleRate, randomValue }) so it always returns true for errors, and otherwise returns true only when randomValue < sampleRate.

tests.description: always keeps errors even with a very high randomValue
drops a success above the sample rate
keeps a success below the sample rate

items.explanation: Checking isError first and short-circuiting to true is what guarantees a failure is never dropped by sampling — the probability check only ever applies to the routine, successful case.
items.reference:
🚨 Failures — always kept, regardless of sample rate
🎲 Successes — kept only with probability sampleRate

Why: this keeps every request that actually matters for debugging while thinning out the routine, already-understood volume.

items.prompt: Implement estimateKeptFraction(sampleRate, errorRate) that returns the fraction of all requests expected to be kept: all the errors, plus sampleRate of the non-error requests. Assume errorRate and sampleRate are both between 0 and 1.

tests.description: with no errors, kept fraction equals the sample rate
with all errors, kept fraction is 1 regardless of sample rate
mixed case combines both parts

items.explanation: The kept fraction is the error share (always kept) plus the sampled share of whatever's left over (the non-error requests) — this is the arithmetic behind why a low sample rate still captures 100% of failures.
items.reference:
🚨 Failures — always kept, regardless of sample rate
🎲 Successes — kept only with probability sampleRate

Why: this keeps every request that actually matters for debugging while thinning out the routine, already-understood volume.

items.prompt: Implement filterSampled(requests, sampleRate) where each request is { isError, randomValue }. Return only the requests that would be sampled: errors always, successes only if randomValue < sampleRate.

tests.description: keeps all errors
drops a non-error above the sample rate
keeps a mix correctly
tests.expr: expect(filterSampled([{ isError: true, randomValue: 0.9 }, { isError: false, randomValue: 0.01 }, { isError: false, randomValue: 0.9 }], 0.1).length).toBe(2)

items.explanation: Filtering with an isError-or-below-threshold condition applies the same shouldSample logic across a whole batch of requests at once, which is closer to how a real pipeline decides what to keep.
items.reference:
🚨 Failures — always kept, regardless of sample rate
🎲 Successes — kept only with probability sampleRate

Why: this keeps every request that actually matters for debugging while thinning out the routine, already-understood volume.

items.prompt: Implement formatRecord({ level, service, msg, fields }) so it returns an object with level, service, msg, and every key from fields merged in at the top level.

tests.description: includes the base fields
tests.expr: expect(formatRecord({ level: 'error', service: 'payment', msg: 'timeout', fields: {} })).toEqual({ level: 'error', service: 'payment', msg: 'timeout' })

tests.description: merges extra fields at the top level
tests.expr: expect(formatRecord({ level: 'error', service: 'payment', msg: 'timeout', fields: { orderId: '8841' } })).toEqual({ level: 'error', service: 'payment', msg: 'timeout', orderId: '8841' })

items.explanation: Spreading the extra fields at the top level (rather than nesting them under a 'fields' key) is what keeps every field directly and uniformly filterable in a log query, base fields and custom fields alike.
items.reference:
🪧 Required fields — timestamp, level, service, msg
➕ Extra fields — spread in from the caller (orderId, attempt, ...)

Why: a consistent set of fields is what makes a log line filterable and aggregable later, instead of just readable once.

items.prompt: Implement hasRequiredFields(record) that returns true only if the record has non-empty string values for level, service, and msg.

tests.description: true when all three fields are present
false when msg is missing
false when a field is an empty string

items.explanation: A log line missing one of its core fields is exactly the kind of malformed record that silently breaks a filter query later — validating this at write time catches it before it ever reaches storage.
items.reference:
🪧 Required fields — timestamp, level, service, msg
➕ Extra fields — spread in from the caller (orderId, attempt, ...)

Why: a consistent set of fields is what makes a log line filterable and aggregable later, instead of just readable once.

items.prompt: Implement redactField(record, fieldName) that returns a new object identical to record, but with the given fieldName's value replaced with the string "[REDACTED]" if that field exists.

tests.description: redacts an existing field
leaves other fields untouched
does not mutate the original object
tests.expr: expect((() => { const r = { level: 'info', cardNumber: '4111' }; redactField(r, 'cardNumber'); return r.cardNumber; })()).toBe('4111')

items.explanation: Returning a new object instead of mutating the original is what keeps redaction safe to apply right before a log line is written, without risking corrupting a record another part of the system still holds a reference to — and sensitive fields (card numbers, tokens) genuinely need this step before anything reaches storage.
